danish.title: Tolvte bog (1812) — Kapitel 14
paragraphs: Da fyrstinde Marja (Prins Andrejs søster) hørte fra Nikolaj (Rostov), at hendes bror var hos Rostov-familien i Jaroslavl, begyndte hun straks at forberede sig på at rejse derhen trods sin tantes forsøg på at tale hende fra det — og ikke blot at rejse selv, men at tage sin nevø med. Om det var vanskeligt eller let, muligt eller umuligt, spurgte hun ikke om og ville ikke vide: det var hendes pligt, ikke blot over for sig selv, at være nær sin bror, der måske lå for døden, men at gøre alt for at bringe hans søn til ham, og så begyndte hun at forberede sig. At hun ikke havde hørt fra fyrst Andrej selv tilskrev fyrstinde Marja det, at han var for svag til at skrive, eller at han anså den lange rejse for at være for hård og for farlig for hende og hans søn.

I løbet af få dage var fyrstinde Marja klar til at rejse. Hendes vogne bestod af den store familiekaret, som hun havde rejst til Voronezj i, en halvåben vogn og en bagagevogn. Med hende rejste frøken Bourienne, lille Nikolaj og hans huslærer, hendes gamle amme, tre tjenestepiger, Tikhon og en ung fodmand og kurer, som hendes tante havde sendt med som ledsager.

Den sædvanlige rute gennem Moskva var utænkelig, og den omvej fyrstinde Marja var nødt til at tage gennem Lipetsk, Rjazan, Vladimir og Sjuja var meget lang og — da der ikke overalt kunne skaffes postheste — meget besværlig, og nær Rjazan, hvor franskmændene efter sigende havde vist sig, var den endda farlig.

Under denne besværlige rejse var frøken Bourienne, Dessalles og fyrstinde Marjas tjenestefolk forbløffede over hendes energi og viljestyrke. Hun gik senere i seng og stod tidligere op end nogen af dem, og ingen vanskeligheder afskrækkede hende. Takket være hendes virksomhed og energi, som smittede hendes rejsefæller, nærmede de sig Jaroslavl ved udgangen af den anden uge.

De sidste dage af hendes ophold i Voronezj havde været de lykkeligste i hendes liv. Hendes kærlighed til Rostov pinte eller uroligede hende ikke længere. Den fyldte hele hendes sjæl, var blevet en del af hende selv, og hun kæmpede ikke længere imod den. I den seneste tid var hun blevet overbevist om, at hun elskede og var elsket, skønt hun aldrig sagde det direkte til sig selv med ord. Hun var blevet overbevist om det ved sit sidste møde med Nikolaj, da han var kommet for at fortælle hende, at hendes bror var hos Rostov-familien. Ikke med et eneste ord havde Nikolaj hentydet til, at fyrst Andrejs forhold til Natasja (Rostova) måske kunne genoptages, hvis han kom sig, men fyrstinde Marja så på hans ansigt, at han vidste det og tænkte på det.

Alligevel var hans holdning til hende — hensynsfuld, fin og kærlig — ikke blot uforandret; det forekom sommetider fyrstinde Marja, at han ligefrem var glad for, at familieforbindelsen mellem dem gav ham mulighed for friere at udtrykke sit venskab. Hun vidste, at hun elskede for første og eneste gang i sit liv, og følte, at hun var elsket, og var lykkelig derved.

Men denne lykke på den ene side af hendes sjæleliv hindrede hende ikke i at føle sorg over sin bror med fuld styrke; tværtimod gjorde den indre ro på den ene side det desto mere muligt for hende at give frit løb for sine følelser for sin bror. Den følelse var så stærk i afrejsens øjeblik fra Voronezj, at de, der så hende af sted, med hendes bekymrede, fortvivlede ansigt, var sikre på, at hun ville blive syg undervejs. Men netop rejsens vanskeligheder og gøremål, som hun tog sig af med så stor iver, reddede hende for en stund fra hendes sorg og gav hende kræfter.

Som det altid sker under rejser, tænkte fyrstinde Marja kun på selve rejsen og glemte dens formål. Men da hun nærmede sig Jaroslavl, trængte tanken om, hvad der måske ventede hende dér — ikke om mange dage, men allerede den aften — sig på ny ind i hendes bevidsthed, og hendes uro voksede til det yderste.

Kureren, der var blevet sendt i forvejen for at finde ud af, hvor Rostov-familien boede i Jaroslavl og i hvilken tilstand fyrst Andrej befandt sig, forfærdedes over den frygtelige bleghed i fyrstindens ansigt, da det viste sig i vinduet, netop som den store karet kørte ind ad byens porte.
»Jeg har fundet ud af alt, Deres excellence: Rostov-familien bor hos købmand Bronnikov, på torvet ikke langt herfra, lige over Volga,« sagde kureren.

Fyrstinde Marja så på ham med et forskrækket, spørgende blik uden at forstå, hvorfor han ikke svarede på det, hun mest af alt ville vide: hvordan havde hendes bror det? Frøken Bourienne stillede spørgsmålet for hende.
»Hvordan har fyrsten det?« spurgte hun.
»Hans excellence bor i det samme hus som dem.«
»Så lever han,« tænkte fyrstinde Marja og spurgte med lav stemme: »Hvordan har han det?«
»Tjenestefolkene siger, at det er uforandret.«

Hvad »uforandret« kunne betyde, spurgte fyrstinde Marja ikke om, men med et ubemærket blik på den lille syvårige Nikolaj, der sad foran hende og med fornøjelse betragtede byen, bøjede hun hovedet og løftede det ikke igen, før den tunge karet med rumlen, rysten og gyngen standsede. Karrettrinene klirrede, da de blev slået ned.

Karetdøren blev åbnet. Til venstre var der vand — en stor flod — og til højre en veranda. Der stod mennesker ved indgangen: tjenestefolk og en rosenkindede pige med en stor, sort fletning, der smilede på en måde, som forekom fyrstinde Marja ubehageligt affekteret. (Det var Sonja.) Fyrstinde Marja løb op ad trappen. »Herind, herind!« sagde pigen med det samme kunstige smil, og fyrstinden befandt sig i forhallen over for en ældre kvinde af orientalsk type, der hurtigt kom hende i møde med et bevæget udtryk. Det var grevinden. Hun omfavnede fyrstinde Marja og kyssede hende.
»Mon enfant!« mumlede hun, »je vous aime et vous connais depuis longtemps.«
»Mit barn! Jeg elsker Dem og har kendt Dem længe.«

Trods sin ophidselse indså fyrstinde Marja, at dette var grevinden, og at det var nødvendigt at sige noget til hende. Næsten uden at vide hvordan lykkedes det hende at fremstamme nogle høflige fraser på fransk i samme tone som dem, der var blevet rettet til hende, og hun spurgte: »Hvordan har han det?«
»Lægen siger, at han ikke er i fare,« sagde grevinden, men idet hun talte, løftede hun øjnene med et suk, og hendes gestus modsagde hendes ord.
»Hvor er han? Kan jeg se ham — kan jeg?« spurgte fyrstinden.

»Et øjeblik, fyrstinde, et øjeblik, min kære! Er det hans søn?« sagde grevinden og vendte sig mod lille Nikolaj, der kom ind med Dessalles. »Der er plads til alle, det er et stort hus. Åh, sikke en dejlig dreng!«

Grevinden førte fyrstinde Marja ind i dagligstuen, hvor Sonja sad og talte med frøken Bourienne. Grevinden kælede for drengen, og den gamle greve kom ind og bød fyrstinden velkommen. Han havde forandret sig meget, siden fyrstinde Marja sidst havde set ham. Dengang havde han været en livlig, munter, selvsikker gammel mand; nu lignede han en ynkværdig, forvirret person. Mens han talte med fyrstinde Marja, kiggede han hele tiden rundt, som om han spurgte alle, om han gjorde det rigtige. Efter Moskvas ødelæggelse og tabet af sin ejendom syntes han, revet ud af sit vante spor, at have mistet følelsen af sin egen betydning og at føle, at der ikke længere var plads til ham i livet.

Trods sit ene ønske om at se sin bror snarest muligt og sin irritation over, at de i dette øjeblik, hvor alt, hvad hun ønskede, var at se ham, forsøgte at underholde hende og lade som om de beundrede hendes nevø, bemærkede fyrstinden alt, hvad der foregik omkring hende, og følte nødvendigheden af for en tid at underkaste sig denne nye tingenes orden, som hun var trådt ind i. Hun vidste, at det var nødvendigt, og skønt det var svært for hende, var hun ikke vred på disse mennesker.
»Det er min niece,« sagde greven og præsenterede Sonja — »De kender hende ikke, fyrstinde?«

Fyrstinde Marja vendte sig mod Sonja og forsøgte at undertrykke den fjendtlige følelse, der rejste sig i hende mod pigen, og kyssede hende. Men hun følte sig trykket af, at stemningen hos alle omkring hende var så fjernt fra det, der fyldte hendes eget hjerte.
»Hvor er han?« spurgte hun igen og henvendte sig til dem alle.
»Han er nedenunder. Natasja er hos ham,« svarede Sonja og rødmede. »Vi har sendt bud. Jeg tror, De må være træt, fyrstinde.«

Tårer af fortvivlelse viste sig i fyrstinde Marjas øjne. Hun vendte sig bort og var ved at spørge grevinden endnu en gang, hvordan hun kom ned til ham, da der hørtes lette, hurtige og tilsyneladende fjederagtige skridt ved døren. Fyrstinden så sig om og fik øje på Natasja, der kom ind næsten løbende — den Natasja, som hun havde syntes så lidt om ved deres møde i Moskva for længe siden.

Men næppe havde fyrstinden set Natasjas ansigt, før hun indså, at her var en sand kammerat i hendes sorg og følgelig en ven. Hun løb hende i møde, omfavnede hende og begyndte at græde mod hendes skulder.

Så snart Natasja, der sad ved hovedgærdet af fyrst Andrejs seng, hørte om fyrstinde Marjas ankomst, forlod hun stille hans værelse og skyndte sig hen til hende med de hurtige skridt, der havde lydt så fjederagtige for fyrstinde Marja.

Der var kun ét udtryk i hendes bevægede ansigt, da hun løb ind i dagligstuen — kærlighedens — grænseløs kærlighed til ham, til hende, og til alt, der var nær det menneske, hun elskede; og medlidenhed, andres lidelse og et lidenskabeligt ønske om at hengive sig helt til at hjælpe dem. Det var tydeligt, at der i det øjeblik ikke var nogen tanke i Natasjas hjerte om hende selv eller om hendes eget forhold til fyrst Andrej.
Fyrstinde Marja forstod med sin fine følsomhed alt dette ved det første blik på Natasjas ansigt og græd mod hendes skulder med smertefuld glæde.
»Kom, kom til ham, Masja,« sagde Natasja og førte hende ind i det andet værelse.
Fyrstinde Marja løftede hovedet, tørrede sine øjne og vendte sig mod Natasja. Hun følte, at hun fra hende ville kunne forstå og lære alt.
»Hvordan...« begyndte hun sit spørgsmål, men stoppede.
Hun følte, at det var umuligt at spørge eller svare med ord. Natasjas ansigt og øjne måtte fortælle hende alt langt tydeligere og dybere.

Natasja stirrede på hende, men syntes bange og i tvivl om, hvorvidt hun skulle sige alt, hvad hun vidste; hun syntes at føle, at det over for disse strålende øjne, der trængte ind i selve hjertets dyb, var umuligt ikke at fortælle hele sandheden, som hun så den. Og pludselig sitrede Natasjas læber, grimme rynker samlede sig om hendes mund, og hun dækkede ansigtet med hænderne og brast i gråd.
Fyrstinde Marja forstod.
Men hun håbede stadig og spurgte med ord, hun selv ikke troede på:
»Men hvordan er hans sår? Hvordan er hans tilstand i det hele taget?«
»De, De... vil se,« var alt, Natasja kunne sige.
De sad en stund nedenunder nær hans værelse, indtil de var holdt op med at græde og kunne gå ind til ham med rolige ansigter.
»Hvordan har hele hans sygdom forløbet? Er det længe siden, han blev værre? Hvornår skete det?« spurgte fyrstinde Marja.

Natasja fortalte hende, at der i begyndelsen havde været fare på grund af hans febertilstand og de smerter, han led, men at det var gået over ved Troitsa, og at lægen kun havde frygtet koldbrand. Den fare var også overstået. Da de nåede Jaroslavl, var såret begyndt at bulne (Natasja vidste alt om sådanne ting som betændelse), og lægen havde sagt, at betændelsen muligvis ville forløbe normalt. Derefter var der kommet feber, men lægen havde sagt, at feberen ikke var alvorlig.
»Men for to dage siden skete det pludselig,« sagde Natasja og kæmpede med sin hulken. »Jeg ved ikke hvorfor, men De vil se, hvordan han er.«
»Er han svagere? Tyndere?« spurgte fyrstinden.
»Nej, det er ikke det, men værre. De vil se. Å, Masja, han er for god, han kan ikke, kan ikke leve, fordi...«

english.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: When Princess Mary heard from Nicholas that her brother was with the Rostovs at Yaroslavl, she prepared at once to go there, despite her aunt's efforts to talk her out of it. She meant not only to go herself but to take her nephew with her. She did not ask whether it would be hard or easy, possible or impossible, and did not want to know. It was her duty not only to be near her brother, who might be dying, but to do everything she could to bring his son to him, so she got ready to leave. She put down the fact that she had not heard from Prince Andrew himself to his being too weak to write, or to his thinking the long journey too hard and too dangerous for her and his son.

Within a few days Princess Mary was ready to start. She traveled in the huge family coach that had taken her to Voronezh, with a half-open trap and a baggage cart following. With her traveled Mademoiselle Bourienne, little Nicholas and his tutor, her old nurse, three maids, Tikhon, and a young footman and courier whom her aunt had sent along with her.

Going the usual way, through Moscow, was out of the question. The roundabout road she had to take, through Lipetsk, Ryazan, Vladimir and Shuya, was very long. Post horses were not to be had everywhere, so it was also very difficult, and near Ryazan, where the French were said to have shown themselves, it was even dangerous.

During this difficult journey Mademoiselle Bourienne, Dessalles and Princess Mary's servants were amazed at her energy and strength of spirit. She stayed up later and rose earlier than any of them, and no difficulty put her off. Her activity and energy rubbed off on her fellow travelers, and by the end of the second week they were nearing Yaroslavl.

She had spent her last days in Voronezh in the happiest time of her life. Her love for Rostov no longer tormented or unsettled her. It filled her whole soul, it had become part of her, and she no longer fought against it. Lately she had become convinced that she loved and was loved, though she never spelled this out to herself in words. The conviction had come at her last meeting with Nicholas, when he came to tell her that her brother was with the Rostovs. Nicholas had not said a single word about the possibility that Prince Andrew's relations with Natasha might be renewed if he recovered, but Princess Mary saw from his face that he knew it and thought about it.

Yet even so, he treated her just as before — considerately, delicately, lovingly. Sometimes it even seemed to Princess Mary that he was glad the family connection between them allowed him to show his friendship more freely. She knew she was loving for the first and only time in her life, and she felt that she was loved, and she was happy about it.

But the happiness in one part of her soul did not stop her from feeling her grief for her brother with full force. On the contrary, the peace she had found there made it easier to let her feeling for her brother run free. At the moment she left Voronezh it was so strong that the people seeing her off took one look at her careworn, despairing face and felt sure she would fall ill on the way. But the very difficulties and worries of the journey, which she took in hand so actively, saved her for a time from her grief and gave her strength.

As always happens on a journey, Princess Mary thought only of the traveling itself and forgot where it led. But as she drew near Yaroslavl, the thought of what might be waiting for her there came back — and not after many days, but that very evening. Her agitation rose to its highest pitch.

The courier had been sent ahead to find out where the Rostovs were staying in Yaroslavl and how Prince Andrew was. He met the big coach just as it was entering the town gates, and he was appalled by the terrible pallor of the princess's face looking out at him from the window.
"I've found out everything, Your Excellency: the Rostovs are staying at the merchant Bronnikov's house, in the Square not far from here, right above the Volga," said the courier.

Princess Mary looked at him with frightened inquiry. She did not understand why he had not answered what she most wanted to know: how was her brother? Mademoiselle Bourienne asked that question for her.
"How is the prince?" she asked.
"His Excellency is staying in the same house with them."
"Then he is alive," thought Princess Mary, and she asked in a low voice, "How is he?"
"The servants say he is still the same."

Princess Mary did not ask what "still the same" might mean. With an unnoticed glance at little seven-year-old Nicholas, who sat in front of her looking at the town with pleasure, she bowed her head and did not raise it again until the heavy coach, rumbling, shaking and swaying, came to a stop. The carriage steps clattered as they were let down.

The carriage door opened. On the left there was water — a great river — and on the right a porch. There were people at the entrance: servants, and a rosy girl with a large plait of black hair, who smiled in a way that struck Princess Mary as unpleasantly affected. (This was Sonya.) Princess Mary ran up the steps. "This way, this way!" said the girl, with the same artificial smile, and the princess found herself in the hall facing an elderly woman of Oriental type, who came quickly toward her with a look of emotion. This was the countess. She embraced Princess Mary and kissed her.
"Mon enfant!" she murmured, "je vous aime et vous connais depuis longtemps." *
* "My child! I love you and have known you a long time."

Despite her agitation, Princess Mary realized that this was the countess and that she had to say something to her. Hardly knowing how she did it, she managed to utter a few polite phrases in French, in the same tone as those that had been addressed to her, and asked, "How is he?"
"The doctor says he is not in danger," said the countess, but as she spoke she raised her eyes with a sigh, and the gesture contradicted her words.
"Where is he? Can I see him — can I?" asked the princess.

"One moment, Princess, one moment, my dear! Is this his son?" said the countess, turning to little Nicholas, who was coming in with Dessalles. "There will be room for everybody, it's a big house. Oh, what a lovely boy!"

The countess took Princess Mary into the drawing room, where Sonya was talking to Mademoiselle Bourienne. The countess caressed the boy, and the old count came in and welcomed the princess. He had changed very much since Princess Mary had last seen him. Then he had been a brisk, cheerful, self-assured old man. Now he seemed a pitiful, bewildered one. While he talked to Princess Mary he kept looking around as if asking everyone whether he was doing the right thing. After the destruction of Moscow and of his property, thrown out of his accustomed groove, he seemed to have lost the sense of his own importance and to feel that there was no longer a place for him in life.

She had only one desire, to see her brother as soon as possible, and she was vexed that at the very moment when that was all she wanted, they were trying to entertain her and pretending to admire her nephew. Even so, the princess noticed everything going on around her and felt she had to submit, for a time, to this new order of things she had entered. She knew it was necessary, and though it was hard for her she was not angry with these people.
"This is my niece," said the count, introducing Sonya. "You don't know her, Princess?"

Princess Mary turned to Sonya and, trying to stifle the hostile feeling that rose in her toward the girl, she kissed her. But it weighed on her that everyone around her was in a mood so far from what filled her own heart.
"Where is he?" she asked again, addressing them all.
"He is downstairs. Natasha is with him," answered Sonya, blushing. "We've sent to ask. I think you must be tired, Princess."

Tears of vexation came into Princess Mary's eyes. She turned away and was about to ask the countess again how to get to him, when light, impetuous and seemingly buoyant steps were heard at the door. The princess looked round and saw Natasha come in, almost running — the same Natasha she had liked so little when they met in Moscow long ago.

But hardly had the princess looked at Natasha's face when she realized that here was a true companion in her grief, and therefore a friend. She ran to meet her, embraced her and began to cry on her shoulder.

As soon as Natasha, sitting at the head of Prince Andrew's bed, heard of Princess Mary's arrival, she softly left his room and hurried to her with those swift steps that had sounded buoyant to Princess Mary.

Her agitated face had only one expression when she ran into the drawing room: love — boundless love for him, for Mary, and for everything that was close to the man she loved; and pity, suffering for others, and a passionate desire to give herself entirely to helping them. It was plain that at that moment Natasha had no thought in her heart of herself or of her own relations with Prince Andrew.
Princess Mary, with her acute sensibility, understood all this at the first glance at Natasha's face, and wept on her shoulder with sorrowful pleasure.
"Come, come to him, Mary," said Natasha, leading her into the other room.
Princess Mary raised her head, dried her eyes and turned to Natasha. She felt that from her she would be able to understand and learn everything.
"How..." she began her question but stopped short.
She felt that it was impossible to ask or to answer in words. Natasha's face and eyes would have to tell her everything, more clearly and more deeply.

Natasha was looking at her, but seemed afraid and unsure whether to say all she knew. She seemed to feel that before those luminous eyes, which penetrated into the very depths of her heart, it was impossible not to tell the whole truth she saw. And suddenly Natasha's lips twitched, ugly wrinkles gathered around her mouth, and covering her face with her hands she burst into sobs.
Princess Mary understood.
Still, she hoped, and she asked in words she herself did not trust:
"But how is his wound? What is his general condition?"
"You, you... will see," was all Natasha could say.
They sat for a little while downstairs near his room until they had stopped crying and could go to him with calm faces.
"How has his whole illness gone? Did he get worse long ago? When did this happen?" Princess Mary asked.

Natasha told her that at first his fever and pain had put him in danger, but at Troitsa that had passed, and the doctor had only feared gangrene. That danger had passed too. When they reached Yaroslavl the wound had begun to fester (Natasha knew all about such things as festering), and the doctor had said that the festering might take a normal course. Then a fever set in, but the doctor had said the fever was not very serious.
"But two days ago this suddenly happened," said Natasha, struggling with her sobs. "I don't know why, but you will see what he is like."
"Is he weaker? Thinner?" asked the princess.
"No, it's not that, but worse. You will see. Oh, Mary, he is too good, he cannot, cannot live, because..."
